Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

The printed form and the website ask for the same information, but the questions are not in the same order. That is making a few customers call the shop to check whether they have missed a step. Mara, who manages the bakery, says the form should feel straightforward even to someone placing an order for the first time. I usually think the printed version is easier to follow, though perhaps that is because I see it at the counter each week.

The first section asks for a customer’s name, phone number, and email address, followed by the date the order is needed. At present, the date field is small, and people sometimes write the pickup time where the date should go. The bakery is open Tuesday through Sunday, from 7 a.m. until 4 p.m., and it does not take Monday pickups. Mara asked for the available pickup days to be listed beside the date field instead of being explained in a note at the bottom. The form also asks whether the customer wants to be contacted by phone or email if staff need to clarify a detail. “We don’t want to guess about a cake message,” Mara said. That choice should remain optional, since most orders do not need a follow-up.

Pickup timing matters because the small front refrigerator has limited room, and decorated cakes are kept in the back until they are due to be collected. The customer can choose a time in half-hour increments, from 9 a.m. to 3:30 p.m. The bakery cannot promise a pickup outside those hours. If an order is for a same-day pickup, the customer must call before placing it online; the website form is intended for orders placed at least one day ahead. That condition is easy to miss in the current version, where it appears after the payment details. Mara would like it next to the pickup date, where it can be seen before a customer chooses a time.

The product section needs to show the choices more clearly, without suggesting that every item can be customized in every way. The regular menu includes round cakes in six-inch and nine-inch sizes, a rectangular sheet cake, cupcakes by the dozen, and two kinds of cookie boxes. The cake flavors are vanilla, chocolate, lemon, and carrot. Buttercream is available in vanilla or chocolate, while the carrot cake comes with cream cheese frosting only. The form currently puts frosting choices beneath all the flavors, which has led to requests for chocolate frosting on carrot cake. Mara said, “We can make the options clear without making the page feel like a rulebook.” The form should say that frosting selection applies to vanilla, chocolate, and lemon cakes, and that carrot cake has cream cheese frosting.

1. For a round cake, the customer should mark one size and one flavor. The six-inch cake serves about eight people, and the nine-inch one serves about eighteen. Those serving counts are estimates, not guarantees, because slices vary in size. The sheet cake is listed as serving about twenty-four, and cupcakes are sold by the dozen, with a minimum order of one dozen. Cookie boxes come in a dozen or two dozen, and the choices are oatmeal raisin or chocolate chip. The customer can request a mix of cookie types in the notes, but the bakery may need to call if the requested split is unclear. These quantities should be shown next to each item rather than collected in a general notes field.

The allergy question is currently a blank line labeled “special requests,” which is too broad to help staff sort the information. The revised form should ask whether the order needs an allergy note and provide room to name the ingredient. Juniper Street Bakery uses wheat, eggs, milk, peanuts, and tree nuts in its kitchen, and it cannot promise that an item is free of traces from shared equipment. Mara wants the form to state that limitation plainly, while still allowing customers to tell the bakery about an allergy. “Please don’t make it sound like we can guarantee a safe product,” she said. This note belongs beside the allergy field, not in tiny print at the end. Customers can also use the same space for a non-allergy dietary question, but the bakery will contact them before confirming whether it can meet that request.

For celebration cakes, the form has a separate message box with room for up to thirty characters, including spaces. The staff can write a short message in icing, but they do not offer custom drawings through the order form. Customers can choose a border color from white, pink, blue, or green, and can ask for no border. The color is a request rather than a promise, because the shade may look slightly different on different frosting. If someone needs a particular color for an event, Mara prefers that they call the bakery to discuss it before submitting the order. The form should keep the message and border choices together, but it should not imply that the message can be longer than the character limit or that a drawing is available.

Payment is due when the customer places the order, either at the counter or through the website. The shop accepts cash and card at the counter, and the website accepts card only. The current printed form asks for payment details before customers have selected their products, which can feel out of order. Mara would rather move payment to the last section. Orders can be changed up to 48 hours before pickup by calling the shop; after that point, staff may not be able to change the product or message. If a customer cancels at least 48 hours before pickup, the payment is refunded. The form should distinguish that cancellation condition from a late change, since the two requests do not have the same result.

Once a form is received, the counter staff copy the order date and pickup time onto the daily sheet, while the baker checks the flavors, quantities, and any allergy note. The daily sheet has space for twelve orders, so a busy Saturday may take more than one page. The bakery uses paper forms at the counter because some customers prefer not to order online, and those forms are kept in a drawer beside the receipt printer until they are entered on the sheet. The website sends a confirmation email after submission, but the printed form does not create an automatic confirmation. Staff tell counter customers their order details aloud before taking payment, which gives them a chance to catch a mistaken date or phone number.

The packaging question should remain near the end of the form. Customers can request a cake box with a window, a plain cake box, or separate cupcake carriers, depending on what they order. The bakery does not currently offer reusable containers, and customers cannot bring their own packaging for an order placed through the website. At the counter, a customer can ask about bringing a clean container before placing the order, but staff need to check whether it fits the item. Mara says the packaging choices are useful, but she would keep the wording brief so customers do not mistake them for different product sizes.
